claim: The generation time distribution characterises changes in the transmission risk during SARS-CoV-2 infections.
source: The distribution of the generation time (the interval between individuals becoming infected and transmitting the virus) characterises changes in the transmission risk during SARS-CoV-2 infections.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the generation time distribution presented in the abstract.

claim: Inferring the generation time distribution is essential to plan and assess public health measures.
source: Inferring the generation time distribution is essential to plan and assess public health measures.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of generation time estimation for public health policy.

claim: A mechanistic approach for estimating the generation time provided an improved fit to data from the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic (December 2019-March 2020) compared to existing models.
source: We previously developed a mechanistic approach for estimating the generation time, which provided an improved fit to data from the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic (December 2019-March 2020) compared to existing models (Hart et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Hart et al., 2021.

claim: Few estimates of the generation time exist based on data from later in the pandemic.
source: However, few estimates of the generation time exist based on data from later in the pandemic.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of the study.

claim: The household study was conducted from March to November 2020 in the UK.
source: Here, using data from a household study conducted from March to November 2020 in the UK, we provide updated estimates of the generation time.
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study.

claim: Assuming independent transmission and symptoms, the mean generation time was estimated to be 4.2 days (95% credible interval 3.3–5.3 days).
source: Assuming independent transmission and symptoms, we estimated a mean generation time (4.2 days, 95% credible interval 3.3–5.3 days) similar to previous estimates from other countries, but with a higher standard deviation (4.9 days, 3.0–8.3 days).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the independent transmission and symptoms model, supported by the data analysis.

claim: Assuming independent transmission and symptoms, the standard deviation of the generation time distribution was estimated to be 4.9 days (95% credible interval 3.0–8.3 days).
source: Assuming independent transmission and symptoms, we estimated a mean generation time (4.2 days, 95% credible interval 3.3–5.3 days) similar to previous estimates from other countries, but with a higher standard deviation (4.9 days, 3.0–8.3 days).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the independent transmission and symptoms model, supported by the data analysis.

claim: Using the mechanistic approach, the mean generation time was estimated to be 5.9 days (95% credible interval 5.2–7.0 days).
source: Using our mechanistic approach, we estimated a longer mean generation time (5.9 days, 5.2–7.0 days) and a similar standard deviation (4.8 days, 4.0–6.3 days).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mechanistic model, supported by the data analysis.

claim: Using the mechanistic approach, the standard deviation of the generation time distribution was estimated to be 4.8 days (95% credible interval 4.0–6.3 days).
source: Using our mechanistic approach, we estimated a longer mean generation time (5.9 days, 5.2–7.0 days) and a similar standard deviation (4.8 days, 4.0–6.3 days).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mechanistic model, supported by the data analysis.

claim: Both models suggest a shorter mean generation time in September-November 2020 compared to earlier months.
source: Both models suggest a shorter mean generation time in September-November 2020 compared to earlier months.
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis of the data using both models.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 generation time appears to be changing.
source: Since the SARS-CoV-2 generation time appears to be changing, further data collection and analysis is necessary to continue to monitor ongoing transmission and inform future public health policy decisions.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal variation observed in the data analysis.

claim: The generation time of a SARS-CoV-2 infector-infectee pair is defined as the period of time between the infector and infectee each becoming infected.
source: The generation time (or generation interval) of a SARS-CoV-2 infector-infectee pair is defined as the period of time between the infector and infectee each becoming infected (Anderson and May, 1992; Diekmann and Heesterbeek, 2000; Griffin et al., 2020; Svensson, 2007; Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: The generation time distribution characterises the temporal profile of the transmission risk of an infected host.
source: The generation time distribution of many infector-infectee pairs characterises the temporal profile of the transmission risk of an infected host (averaged over all hosts and normalised so that it represents a valid probability distribution; Fraser, 2007).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citation to Fraser, 2007.

claim: Inferring the generation time distribution of SARS-CoV-2 is important in order to predict the effects of non-pharmaceutical interventions such as contact tracing and quarantine.
source: Inferring the generation time distribution of SARS-CoV-2 is important in order to predict the effects of non-pharmaceutical interventions such as contact tracing and quarantine (Ashcroft et al., 2021; Ferretti et al., 2020b; Hart et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The generation time distribution is widely used in epidemiological models for estimating the time-dependent reproduction number from case notification data.
source: In addition, the generation time distribution is widely used in epidemiological models for estimating the time-dependent reproduction number from case notification data (Abbott et al., 2020; Fraser, 2007; Gostic et al., 2020; Thompson et al., 2020) and is crucial for understanding the relationship between the reproduction number and the epidemic growth rate (Fraser, 2007; Parag et al., 2021; Park et al., 2020a; Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The generation time distribution is crucial for understanding the relationship between the reproduction number and the epidemic growth rate.
source: In addition, the generation time distribution is widely used in epidemiological models for estimating the time-dependent reproduction number from case notification data (Abbott et al., 2020; Fraser, 2007; Gostic et al., 2020; Thompson et al., 2020) and is crucial for understanding the relationship between the reproduction number and the epidemic growth rate (Fraser, 2007; Parag et al., 2021; Park et al., 2020a; Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 generation time distribution has previously been estimated using data from known infector-infectee transmission pairs.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 generation time distribution has previously been estimated using data from known infector-infectee transmission pairs (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ferretti et al., 2020b; Hart et al., 2021) or entire clusters of cases (Ganyani et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 generation time distribution has previously been estimated using data from entire clusters of cases.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 generation time distribution has previously been estimated using data from known infector-infectee transmission pairs (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ferretti et al., 2020b; Hart et al., 2021) or entire clusters of cases (Ganyani et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Previous studies estimating the SARS-CoV-2 generation time involved data collected between December 2019 and April 2020.
source: These studies involved data (Cheng et al., 2020; Ferretti et al., 2020b; Ganyani et al., 2020; He et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020) collected between December 2019 and April 2020, almost entirely from countries in East and Southeast Asia (with the exception of four transmission pairs from Germany and four from Italy in Ferretti et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Previous studies estimating the SARS-CoV-2 generation time involved data almost entirely from countries in East and Southeast Asia.
source: These studies involved data (Cheng et al., 2020; Ferretti et al., 2020b; Ganyani et al., 2020; He et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020) collected between December 2019 and April 2020, almost entirely from countries in East and Southeast Asia (with the exception of four transmission pairs from Germany and four from Italy in Ferretti et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Evidence from January and February 2020 in China suggested a temporal reduction in the mean generation time due to non-pharmaceutical interventions.
source: Evidence from January and February 2020 in China suggested a temporal reduction in the mean generation time due to non-pharmaceutical interventions (Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2021.

claim: Effective isolation of infected individuals is likely to have reduced the proportion of transmissions occurring when potential infectors were in the later stages of infection, thereby shortening the generation time.
source: Specifically, effective isolation of infected individuals is likely to have reduced the proportion of transmissions occurring when potential infectors were in the later stages of infection, thereby shortening the generation time (Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2021.

claim: Two studies found a decrease in the serial interval in China over January and February 2020.
source: Similarly, two other studies found a decrease in the serial interval (the difference between symptom onset times of an infector and infectee; Ali et al., 2020) and an increase in the proportion of presymptomatic transmissions (Bushman et al., 2021) in China over the same time period, which can be attributed to symptomatic hosts being isolated increasingly quickly over time.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ali et al., 2020.

claim: Two studies found an increase in the proportion of presymptomatic transmissions in China over January and February 2020.
source: Similarly, two other studies found a decrease in the serial interval (the difference between symptom onset times of an infector and infectee; Ali et al., 2020) and an increase in the proportion of presymptomatic transmissions (Bushman et al., 2021) in China over the same time period, which can be attributed to symptomatic hosts being isolated increasingly quickly over time.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bushman et al., 2021.

claim: Relatively little is known about the generation time distribution outside Asia.
source: Despite estimation of the SARS-CoV-2 generation time in Asia early in the pandemic, relatively little is known about the generation time distribution outside Asia, and whether or not any changes have occurred in the generation time since the early months of the pandemic.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge at the time of the study.

claim: Only one previous study estimated the generation time using data from the UK.
source: At the time of writing, we are aware of only one previous study in which the generation time was estimated using data from the UK (Challen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the literature supported by citation to Challen et al., 2021.

claim: In the Challen et al., 2021 study, data describing symptom onset dates for 50 infector-infectee pairs were used to infer the generation time distribution.
source: In that study (Challen et al., 2021), data describing symptom onset dates for 50 infector-infectee pairs, collected by Public Health England (PHE; now the UK Health Security Agency) between January and March 2020 as part of the 'First Few Hundred' case protocol (Boddington et al., 2021; Public Health England, 2020), were used to infer the generation time distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Challen et al., 2021.

claim: The Challen et al., 2021 study authors concluded that their estimates of the generation time may have been biased downwards due to enhanced surveillance and isolation of cases.
source: However, since these transmission pairs mostly consisted of international travellers and their household contacts, the authors concluded that their estimates of the generation time may have been biased downwards due to enhanced surveillance and isolation of these cases (Challen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Challen et al., 2021.

claim: Data were obtained from a household study conducted in 172 UK households between March and November 2020.
source: Here, we use data from a household study (Miller et al., 2021), conducted between March and November 2020, to estimate the SARS-CoV-2 generation time distribution in the UK under two different underlying transmission models.
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study, supported by citation to Miller et al., 2021.

claim: In the independent transmission and symptoms model, a parsimonious assumption is made that the generation time and the incubation period of the infector are independent.
source: In the first model (the 'independent transmission and symptoms model'), a parsimonious assumption is made that the generation time and the incubation period of the infector are independent (i.e. there is no link between the times at which infectors transmit the virus and the times at which they develop symptoms), as has often been employed in studies in which the SARS-CoV-2 generation time has been estimated (Challen et al., 2021; Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ganyani et al., 2020; Hart et al., 2021; Lehtinen et al., 2021; Table 1).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach and is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In the mechanistic model, potential infectors progress through different stages of infection, first becoming infectious before developing symptoms.
source: In the second model (the 'mechanistic model'), we use a mechanistic approach in which potential infectors progress through different stages of infection, first becoming infectious before developing symptoms (Hart et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach and is supported by citation to Hart et al., 2021.

claim: In the mechanistic model, infectiousness is explicitly linked to symptoms.
source: Infectiousness is therefore explicitly linked to symptoms in the mechanistic model.
evidence: This describes a feature of the mechanistic model.

claim: In the mechanistic model, individuals with longer incubation periods will (on average) be infectious for longer before developing symptoms compared to those with shorter incubation periods.
source: A feature of the mechanistic model is that individuals with longer incubation periods will (on average) be infectious for longer before developing symptoms, and so generate more transmissions, compared to those with shorter incubation periods.
evidence: This describes a feature of the mechanistic model.

claim: Ferretti et al., 2020b estimated a mean generation time of 5.0 days using data from various locations during December 2019-February 2020.
source: Ferretti et al., 2020b	Various	December 2019-February 2020	5.0	1.9
evidence: This is data from Table 1 showing previous generation time estimates.

claim: Ganyani et al., 2020 estimated a mean generation time of 5.20 days (3.78–6.78) using data from Singapore during January-February 2020.
source: Ganyani et al., 2020	Singapore	January-February 2020	5.20 (3.78–6.78)	1.72 (0.91–3.93)
evidence: This is data from Table 1 showing previous generation time estimates.

claim: Ganyani et al., 2020 estimated a mean generation time of 3.95 days (3.01–4.91) using data from China during January-February 2020.
source: Ganyani et al., 2020	China	January-February 2020	3.95 (3.01–4.91)	1.51 (0.74–2.97)
evidence: This is data from Table 1 showing previous generation time estimates.

claim: Hart et al., 2021 estimated a mean generation time of 5.57 days (5.08–6.09) using data from various locations during December 2019-March 2020.
evidence: This is data from Table 1 showing previous generation time estimates.

claim: Challen et al., 2021 estimated a mean generation time of 4.8 days (4.3–5.41) using data from the UK during January-March 2020.
source: Challen et al., 2021	UK	January-March 2020	4.8 (4.3–5.41)	1.7 (1.0–2.6)
evidence: This is data from Table 1 showing previous generation time estimates.

claim: Each household was recruited to the study following a confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Each household was recruited to the study following a confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, and all household members were then followed to investigate whether or not they became infected (this was determined through PCR and antibody testing).
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: Infection status was determined through PCR and antibody testing.
source: Each household was recruited to the study following a confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, and all household members were then followed to investigate whether or not they became infected (this was determined through PCR and antibody testing).
evidence: This describes the study methodology.

claim: Data augmentation MCMC was used to account for uncertainty about exactly who-infected-whom within a household.
source: This enabled us (in the likelihood function) to account for uncertainty about exactly who-infected-whom within a household by summing together likelihood contributions corresponding to infection by different possible infectors.
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology used in the study.

claim: The approach corrected for the regularity of household contacts to derive more widely applicable estimates of the generation time.
source: In addition, we corrected for the regularity of household contacts to derive more widely applicable estimates of the generation time.
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the study.

claim: Under the independent transmission and symptoms model, the point estimate of the mean generation time was 4.2 days (95% CrI 3.3–5.3 days).
source: Under the commonly used independent transmission and symptoms model, we obtained a point estimate of 4.2 days (95% credible interval (CrI) 3.3–5.3 days) for the mean generation time (Figure 1A, blue violin; we calculated point estimates for each model using the posterior means of fitted model parameters because the mode of the joint posterior distribution could not easily be calculated from the output of the MCMC procedure).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The mean generation time estimate of 4.2 days is similar to a previous estimate obtained using data from China by Ganyani et al., 2020.
source: This value is similar to a previous estimate obtained using data from China by Ganyani et al., 2020.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature supported by citation.

claim: The estimated standard deviation of 4.9 days (95% CrI 3.0–8.3 days) is substantially higher than previous estimates.
source: On the other hand, our estimated standard deviation of 4.9 days (95% CrI 3.0–8.3 days; Figure 1B, blue violin) is substantially higher than previous estimates (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis compared to previous literature, shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: Using the mechanistic model, the mean generation time was estimated to be 5.9 days (95% CrI 5.2–7.0 days).
source: Using our mechanistic model, we obtained a higher estimate for the mean generation time of 5.9 days (95% CrI 5.2–7.0 days; Figure 1A, red violin), and a similar estimate for the standard deviation (4.8 days, 95% CrI 4.0–6.3 days; Figure 1B, red violin), compared to those predicted by the independent transmission and symptoms model.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Using the mechanistic model, the standard deviation of the generation time distribution was estimated to be 4.8 days (95% CrI 4.0–6.3 days).
source: Using our mechanistic model, we obtained a higher estimate for the mean generation time of 5.9 days (95% CrI 5.2–7.0 days; Figure 1A, red violin), and a similar estimate for the standard deviation (4.8 days, 95% CrI 4.0–6.3 days; Figure 1B, red violin), compared to those predicted by the independent transmission and symptoms model.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The proportion of transmissions occurring prior to symptom onset was estimated to be 0.72 (95% CrI 0.63–0.80) for the independent transmission and symptoms model.
source: Specifically, point estimate values of model parameters led to an estimated proportion of transmissions prior to symptom onset of 0.72 (95% CrI 0.63–0.80) for the independent transmission and symptoms model, and 0.73 (95% CrI 0.61–0.83) for the mechanistic model.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The proportion of transmissions occurring prior to symptom onset was estimated to be 0.73 (95% CrI 0.61–0.83) for the mechanistic model.
source: Specifically, point estimate values of model parameters led to an estimated proportion of transmissions prior to symptom onset of 0.72 (95% CrI 0.63–0.80) for the independent transmission and symptoms model, and 0.73 (95% CrI 0.61–0.83) for the mechanistic model.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The estimates of the proportion of presymptomatic transmissions are higher than obtained in some previous studies.
source: These estimates are higher than obtained in some previous studies in which the infectiousness profile of SARS-CoV-2 infected hosts at each time since infection and/or time since symptom onset has been estimated (Ashcroft et al., 2020; Ferretti et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature supported by citations.

claim: Realised household generation times are expected to be shorter than the estimates shown in Figure 1 due to the depletion of susceptible household members.
source: However, realised household generation times are expected to be shorter than the estimates shown in Figure 1. This is due to the depletion of susceptible household members before longer generation times can be obtained, especially in small households (Cauchemez et al., 2009; Fraser, 2007; Park et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling approach, supported by citations.

claim: For the independent transmission and symptoms model, the mean of realised generation times within the study households was 3.6 days.
source: For both the independent transmission and symptoms model and the mechanistic model, the mean (point estimates 3.6 days and 4.9 days for the two models, respectively) and standard deviation (3.8 days and 4.1 days) of realised household generation times were lower than our main generation time estimates shown in Figure 1.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: For the mechanistic model, the mean of realised generation times within the study households was 4.9 days.
source: For both the independent transmission and symptoms model and the mechanistic model, the mean (point estimates 3.6 days and 4.9 days for the two models, respectively) and standard deviation (3.8 days and 4.1 days) of realised household generation times were lower than our main generation time estimates shown in Figure 1.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The TOST distribution obtained using the mechanistic model was more concentrated around the time of symptom onset compared to that predicted assuming independent transmission and symptoms.
source: The TOST distribution (which characterises the relative expected infectiousness of a host (who develops symptoms) at each time from symptom onset, as opposed to from infection [Ashcroft et al., 2020; Ferretti et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020; Lehtinen et al., 2021; Wells et al., 2021]) obtained using the mechanistic model was more concentrated around the time of symptom onset compared to that predicted assuming independent transmission and symptoms (Figure 2B), as we found in our previous work (Hart et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 2B, consistent with previous work.

claim: The estimated serial interval distributions were similar for the two models.
source: In contrast, the estimated serial interval distributions were similar for the two models (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: For the independent transmission and symptoms model fitted to March-April data, the mean generation time was estimated to be 4.9 days (95% CrI 3.6–6.3 days).
source: The results shown in Figure 3A suggest a shorter mean generation time in September-November 2020 (2.9 days, 95% CrI 1.8–4.3 days) compared to earlier months (4.9 days, 95% CrI 3.6–6.3 days, for March-April and 5.2 days, 95% CrI 3.4–7.2 days, for May-August).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For the independent transmission and symptoms model fitted to May-August data, the mean generation time was estimated to be 5.2 days (95% CrI 3.4–7.2 days).
source: The results shown in Figure 3A suggest a shorter mean generation time in September-November 2020 (2.9 days, 95% CrI 1.8–4.3 days) compared to earlier months (4.9 days, 95% CrI 3.6–6.3 days, for March-April and 5.2 days, 95% CrI 3.4–7.2 days, for May-August).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For the independent transmission and symptoms model fitted to September-November data, the mean generation time was estimated to be 2.9 days (95% CrI 1.8–4.3 days).
source: The results shown in Figure 3A suggest a shorter mean generation time in September-November 2020 (2.9 days, 95% CrI 1.8–4.3 days) compared to earlier months (4.9 days, 95% CrI 3.6–6.3 days, for March-April and 5.2 days, 95% CrI 3.4–7.2 days, for May-August).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a 97% posterior probability of a shorter mean generation time in September-November compared to May-August.
source: Comparing the posterior estimates for May-August and September-November (the red and orange violins in Figure 3A, respectively) indicated a 97% posterior probability of a shorter mean generation time in the later of these two time periods.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the temporal analysis.

claim: Using the mechanistic model, the mean generation time was estimated to be 6.5 days (95% CrI 5.6–8.1 days) for March-April.
source: Estimates of the mean generation time using the mechanistic model were 6.5 days (95% CrI 5.6–8.1 days) for March-April, 7.1 days (95% CrI 5.7–9.6 days) for May-August, and 5.1 days (95% CrI 4.3–6.4 days) for September-November, with a 98% posterior probability of a shorter mean generation time in September-November than May-August.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis using the mechanistic model.

claim: Using the mechanistic model, the mean generation time was estimated to be 7.1 days (95% CrI 5.7–9.6 days) for May-August.
source: Estimates of the mean generation time using the mechanistic model were 6.5 days (95% CrI 5.6–8.1 days) for March-April, 7.1 days (95% CrI 5.7–9.6 days) for May-August, and 5.1 days (95% CrI 4.3–6.4 days) for September-November, with a 98% posterior probability of a shorter mean generation time in September-November than May-August.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis using the mechanistic model.

claim: Using the mechanistic model, the mean generation time was estimated to be 5.1 days (95% CrI 4.3–6.4 days) for September-November.
source: Estimates of the mean generation time using the mechanistic model were 6.5 days (95% CrI 5.6–8.1 days) for March-April, 7.1 days (95% CrI 5.7–9.6 days) for May-August, and 5.1 days (95% CrI 4.3–6.4 days) for September-November, with a 98% posterior probability of a shorter mean generation time in September-November than May-August.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis using the mechanistic model.

claim: Using the mechanistic model, there was a 98% posterior probability of a shorter mean generation time in September-November than May-August.
source: Estimates of the mean generation time using the mechanistic model were 6.5 days (95% CrI 5.6–8.1 days) for March-April, 7.1 days (95% CrI 5.7–9.6 days) for May-August, and 5.1 days (95% CrI 4.3–6.4 days) for September-November, with a 98% posterior probability of a shorter mean generation time in September-November than May-August.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the temporal analysis.

claim: The proportion of transmissions occurring prior to symptom onset was estimated to be 0.83 (95% CrI 0.72–0.93) in September-November.
source: Figure 3C shows posterior estimates for the proportion of transmissions occurring prior to symptom onset (among symptomatic infectors) across the three time periods for the independent transmission and symptoms model, indicating a very high proportion of presymptomatic transmissions in September-November (0.83, 95% CrI 0.72–0.93) compared to lower estimates for March-April (0.64, 95% CrI 0.51–0.77) and May-August (0.62, 95% CrI 0.41–0.79).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The proportion of transmissions occurring prior to symptom onset was estimated to be 0.64 (95% CrI 0.51–0.77) in March-April.
source: Figure 3C shows posterior estimates for the proportion of transmissions occurring prior to symptom onset (among symptomatic infectors) across the three time periods for the independent transmission and symptoms model, indicating a very high proportion of presymptomatic transmissions in September-November (0.83, 95% CrI 0.72–0.93) compared to lower estimates for March-April (0.64, 95% CrI 0.51–0.77) and May-August (0.62, 95% CrI 0.41–0.79).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The proportion of transmissions occurring prior to symptom onset was estimated to be 0.62 (95% CrI 0.41–0.79) in May-August.
source: Figure 3C shows posterior estimates for the proportion of transmissions occurring prior to symptom onset (among symptomatic infectors) across the three time periods for the independent transmission and symptoms model, indicating a very high proportion of presymptomatic transmissions in September-November (0.83, 95% CrI 0.72–0.93) compared to lower estimates for March-April (0.64, 95% CrI 0.51–0.77) and May-August (0.62, 95% CrI 0.41–0.79).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The Alpha (B.1.1.7) variant had begun to emerge in the UK by the end of the study period.
source: We note that, while the Alpha (B.1.1.7) variant had begun to emerge in the UK by the end of the study period (Public Health England, 2021), genomic surveillance as part of the study showed that this variant caused infections in only two study households.
evidence: This is a statement about the epidemiological context supported by citation.

claim: The Alpha variant caused infections in only two study households.
source: We note that, while the Alpha (B.1.1.7) variant had begun to emerge in the UK by the end of the study period (Public Health England, 2021), genomic surveillance as part of the study showed that this variant caused infections in only two study households.
evidence: This is a finding from genomic surveillance data.

claim: The Alpha variant was unlikely to have been responsible for the temporal reduction in the generation time that was observed.
source: This variant was therefore unlikely to have been responsible for the temporal reduction in the generation time that we observed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low prevalence of the Alpha variant in the study data.

claim: Accounting for the possibility of co-primary cases led to slightly higher estimates of the mean generation time compared to the main analysis.
source: This led to slightly higher estimates of the mean generation time (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A) under each model compared to the corresponding estimates shown in Figure 1A, with point estimates of 4.8 days (95% CrI 3.6–6.3 days) for the independent transmission and symptoms model and 6.8 days (95% CrI 5.7–8.6 days) for the mechanistic model.
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: When accounting for co-primary cases, the probability of co-primary infection was estimated to be 0.17 (95% CrI 0.02–0.33) under the independent transmission and symptoms model.
source: As part of the fitting procedure, we estimated the probability that each household member was infected during the primary transmission event (Figure 1—figure supplement 5E), obtaining point estimates of 0.17 (95% CrI 0.02–0.33) under the independent transmission and symptoms model and 0.27 (95% CrI 0.10–0.41) under the mechanistic model.
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5E.

claim: When accounting for co-primary cases, the probability of co-primary infection was estimated to be 0.27 (95% CrI 0.10–0.41) under the mechanistic model.
source: As part of the fitting procedure, we estimated the probability that each household member was infected during the primary transmission event (Figure 1—figure supplement 5E), obtaining point estimates of 0.17 (95% CrI 0.02–0.33) under the independent transmission and symptoms model and 0.27 (95% CrI 0.10–0.41) under the mechanistic model.
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5E.

claim: The estimated generation time distribution was robust to the assumed relative infectiousness of asymptomatic hosts.
source: We showed that our estimated generation time distribution was robust to the assumed relative infectiousness of infected hosts who remain asymptomatic, αA (Figure 1—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 11.

claim: The estimated generation time distribution was robust to the assumed dependency of transmission on household size.
source: Similarly, while we assumed frequency-dependent household transmission in most of our analyses, we found that the exact relationship between the household size and transmission had little effect on our estimates of the mean and standard deviation of the generation time distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 9 and Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9 and Figure 1—figure supplement 10.

claim: The estimated dependency parameter ρ was 1.0 (95% CrI 0.6–1.5), supporting the assumption of frequency-dependent transmission.
source: When the value ρ was fitted (Figure 1—figure supplement 9D), we estimated a value of 1.0 (95% CrI 0.6–1.5). This supported our assumption of frequency-dependent transmission, although the credible interval was relatively wide.
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9D.

claim: The estimated generation time distribution was robust to the assumed infection status of individuals of unknown infection status.
source: Although the estimates of β0 were affected by this assumption (Figure 1—figure supplement 12D), the estimated generation time distribution was robust to the assumed infection status of these individuals (Figure 1—figure supplement 12A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 12.

claim: One possible explanation for the shorter mean generation time in September-November is a higher proportion of time spent indoors in colder months leading to an increased transmission risk.
source: One possible explanation for this is a higher proportion of time spent indoors in colder months leading to an increased transmission risk, particularly in the early stages of infection before symptoms develop (since symptomatic infected hosts are still likely to self-isolate).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed temporal pattern.

claim: The B.1.177 lineage emerged in Spain in early summer 2020 and became the dominant SARS-CoV lineage in the UK around the beginning of October 2020.
source: For example, the B.1.177 lineage emerged in Spain in early summer 2020, and became the dominant SARS-CoV lineage in the UK around the beginning of October 2020 (Vöhringer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about viral evolution supported by citation.

claim: The Alpha variant was first detected in September 2020 and became dominant in the UK in December 2020.
source: Subsequently, the Alpha (B.1.1.7) variant, which was first detected in September 2020, became dominant in the UK in December 2020 (Public Health England, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about viral evolution supported by citation.

claim: The Alpha variant has been shown to possess different characteristics than earlier variants.
source: The Alpha variant has been shown to possess different characteristics than earlier variants (Davies et al., 2021; Volz et al., 2021), causing an increased epidemic growth rate in the UK that has been attributed to an increase in transmissibility of 43%–90% (Davies et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about viral characteristics supported by citations.

claim: The Alpha variant caused an increased epidemic growth rate in the UK that has been attributed to an increase in transmissibility of 43%–90%.
source: The Alpha variant has been shown to possess different characteristics than earlier variants (Davies et al., 2021; Volz et al., 2021), causing an increased epidemic growth rate in the UK that has been attributed to an increase in transmissibility of 43%–90% (Davies et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about viral transmissibility supported by citation.

claim: Shorter generation times are expected to be over-represented at times when case numbers are rising in data collected from infector-infectee transmission pairs.
source: In data collected from infector-infectee transmission pairs, shorter generation times are expected to be over-represented at times when case numbers are rising (Britton and Scalia Tomba, 2019; Ferretti et al., 2020b; Lehtinen et al., 2021), and vice versa.
evidence: This is a statement about epidemiological bias supported by citations.

claim: National case numbers were mostly increasing in September-October 2020.
source: While we used data from households (rather than transmission pairs) in our analyses, a similar effect may have contributed to our shorter estimated mean generation time for September-November 2020 (national case numbers were mostly increasing in September-October 2020) compared to earlier months of the study (during which case numbers were mostly decreasing; Knock et al., 2021; Pouwels et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about epidemiological context supported by citations.

claim: National case numbers were mostly decreasing during earlier months of the study.
source: While we used data from households (rather than transmission pairs) in our analyses, a similar effect may have contributed to our shorter estimated mean generation time for September-November 2020 (national case numbers were mostly increasing in September-October 2020) compared to earlier months of the study (during which case numbers were mostly decreasing; Knock et al., 2021; Pouwels et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about epidemiological context supported by citations.

claim: The mean generation time was estimated to be similar in November compared to September and October.
source: However, we estimated the mean generation time to be similar in November (when case numbers were mostly decreasing [Knock et al., 2021; Pouwels et al., 2021]) compared to September and October (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), suggesting that this effect of background epidemic dynamics alone did not drive the temporal changes in generation time that we observed.
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: If the mean generation time is shorter than assumed, then the true value of the time-dependent reproduction number is likely to be closer to one than the inferred value.
source: Specifically, if the mean generation time is shorter than assumed, then the true value of the time-dependent reproduction number is likely to be closer to one than the inferred value (Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007), and vice versa.
evidence: This is a statement about epidemiological inference supported by citation.

claim: One advantage of the approach is that it was able to include the contribution of asymptomatic infected hosts to household transmission chains.
source: One advantage of our approach compared to previous studies in which the SARS-CoV-2 generation time has been estimated (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ganyani et al., 2020; Hart et al., 2021) is that we were able to include the contribution of asymptomatic infected hosts to household transmission chains in our analyses.
evidence: This describes a methodological advantage of the study.

claim: The study found an inverse relationship between household size and secondary attack rate.
source: This supported our assumption of frequency-dependent transmission, and is consistent with the finding of an inverse relationship between household size and secondary attack rate in the household study underlying our analyses (Miller et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the household study supported by citation.

claim: The dataset involved a larger sample size than used in most other studies in which the SARS-CoV-2 generation time was estimated.
source: We also note that, while our dataset involved a larger sample size than used in most other studies in which the SARS-CoV-2 generation time was estimated (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ferretti et al., 2020b; Ganyani et al., 2020; Hart et al., 2021), the demographics of the study households may not have been completely representative of the wider population.
evidence: This is a statement about the study design compared to previous literature.

claim: The demographics of the study households may not have been completely representative of the wider population.
source: We also note that, while our dataset involved a larger sample size than used in most other studies in which the SARS-CoV-2 generation time was estimated (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ferretti et al., 2020b; Ganyani et al., 2020; Hart et al., 2021), the demographics of the study households may not have been completely representative of the wider population.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The study demonstrates that changes in the generation time can be detected using data from household studies.
source: Nonetheless, as well as providing updated SARS-CoV-2 generation time estimates, our study demonstrates that changes in the generation time can be detected using data from household studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Data were obtained from 172 UK households with 603 household members in total.
source: Data were obtained from a household study (Miller et al., 2021) conducted in 172 UK households (with 603 household members in total) by PHE between March and November 2020 (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the data source.

claim: In the study, all household members who tested positive in either a PCR or antibody test were assumed to have been infected.
source: In the study, all household members who tested positive in either a PCR or antibody test were assumed to have been infected.
evidence: This describes the study methodology.

claim: All individuals who tested negative for antibodies and did not return a positive PCR test were assumed to have remained uninfected.
source: Conversely, all individuals who tested negative for antibodies and did not return a positive PCR test (i.e. the two PCR tests were either negative or were not carried out) were assumed to have remained uninfected, irrespective of symptom status.
evidence: This describes the study methodology.

claim: For 34 individuals (6% of the study cohort), no antibody test was carried out and any PCR tests were negative.
source: For 34 individuals (6% of the study cohort), no antibody test was carried out and any PCR tests were negative.
evidence: This describes the data characteristics.

claim: Five households were excluded from the analyses.
source: Data from these two households were excluded from our analyses, on the basis that the virus was most likely introduced multiple times into these households. Three other households were also excluded from our analyses because, other than the index cases in each household, all other household members were of unknown infection status (i.e. they were among the individuals for whom no antibody test was carried out and any PCR tests were negative).
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.

claim: The 167 remaining households comprised 587 individuals.
source: Overall, aside from the five excluded households, the 167 remaining households comprised 587 individuals, of whom 330 became infected and developed symptoms, 27 became infected but remained asymptomatic, 200 remained uninfected, and the remaining 30 were of unknown infection status.
evidence: This describes the final dataset used in the analysis.

claim: Of the 587 individuals in the final dataset, 330 became infected and developed symptoms.
source: Overall, aside from the five excluded households, the 167 remaining households comprised 587 individuals, of whom 330 became infected and developed symptoms, 27 became infected but remained asymptomatic, 200 remained uninfected, and the remaining 30 were of unknown infection status.
evidence: This describes the final dataset used in the analysis.

claim: Of the 587 individuals in the final dataset, 27 became infected but remained asymptomatic.
source: Overall, aside from the five excluded households, the 167 remaining households comprised 587 individuals, of whom 330 became infected and developed symptoms, 27 became infected but remained asymptomatic, 200 remained uninfected, and the remaining 30 were of unknown infection status.
evidence: This describes the final dataset used in the analysis.

claim: Of the 587 individuals in the final dataset, 200 remained uninfected.
source: Overall, aside from the five excluded households, the 167 remaining households comprised 587 individuals, of whom 330 became infected and developed symptoms, 27 became infected but remained asymptomatic, 200 remained uninfected, and the remaining 30 were of unknown infection status.
evidence: This describes the final dataset used in the analysis.

claim: Of the 587 individuals in the final dataset, 30 were of unknown infection status.
source: Overall, aside from the five excluded households, the 167 remaining households comprised 587 individuals, of whom 330 became infected and developed symptoms, 27 became infected but remained asymptomatic, 200 remained uninfected, and the remaining 30 were of unknown infection status.
evidence: This describes the final dataset used in the analysis.

claim: Frequency-dependent household transmission was assumed in most analyses.
source: Except where otherwise stated, we considered the generation time distribution assuming a constant supply of susceptibles during infection, f(τ), which corresponds to the normalised expected infectiousness profile and gives a widely applicable generation time estimate (see Discussion).
evidence: This describes the modeling assumption.

claim: The expected infectiousness of an infected host who remained asymptomatic throughout infection was assumed to be a factor αA=0.35 times that of a host who develops symptoms.
source: In most of our analyses, we assumed that the expected infectiousness of an infected host who remained asymptomatic throughout infection was a factor αA=0.35 times that of a host who develops symptoms, at each time since infection (Buitrago-Garcia et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the modeling assumption supported by citation.

claim: A lognormal incubation period distribution with mean 5.8 days and standard deviation 3.1 days was assumed for the independent transmission and symptoms model.
source: For the independent transmission and symptoms model, we assumed a lognormal incubation period distribution with mean 5.8 days and standard deviation 3.1 days (McAloon et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the modeling assumption supported by citation.

claim: For the mechanistic model, a gamma distributed incubation period with the same mean and standard deviation as the lognormal distribution was assumed.
source: For the mechanistic model, we assumed a gamma distributed incubation period with the same mean and standard deviation; this was for mathematical convenience, since the incubation period could then be decomposed into the sum of independent gamma distributed latent and presymptomatic infectious periods.
evidence: This describes the modeling assumption.

claim: The household study was approved by the PHE Research Ethics and Governance Group.
source: The household study was approved by the PHE Research Ethics and Governance Group as part of the portfolio of PHE's enhanced surveillance activities in response to the pandemic.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.
